# Results — Study 486 (Gann Hi-Lo Activator)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **the flip
forecasts trend: when price closes above the activator, a new up-leg begins** — encoded as a
mechanical rule. The activator is a flipping SMA-of-highs / SMA-of-lows line (period = 10, both
SMAs shifted one bar so the flip is knowable on the close of *t*); a long fires on the first bar
that flips the line short→long, entered at the **next close** (one documented lag), and we
measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day return. Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **1234** mechanical flip-up entries pooled across the 5 tapes (period = 10) |
| Timing / costs | activator SMAs shifted **+1 bar** (flip read on the close of *t*); enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per flip |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument trend study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only the
> drift baseline (which is exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes).

## The signal — flip-up vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch flip-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = flip − random.

| horizon | n | flip | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (flip−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 1233 | +17.8 bps | 58% | +2.63 | +14.1 bps | **+3.6 bps** | +15.8 bps | +0.36 | 0.722 |
| 10-day | 1232 | +43.6 bps | 60% | +3.83 | +49.2 bps | **−5.6 bps** | +41.6 bps | −0.39 | 0.694 |
| 20-day | 1228 | +97.9 bps | 65% | +6.20 | +95.8 bps | **+2.1 bps** | +95.9 bps | +0.10 | 0.917 |
| 60-day | 1221 | +252.7 bps | 68% | +6.24 | +314.6 bps | **−61.9 bps** | +250.7 bps | −1.88 | 0.060 |

Read it carefully. The one-sample *t* against zero looks spectacular (**+6.20** at 20 days,
**+6.24** at 60) — but that is **pure beta**: long-only entries on an upward-drifting index
inherit the drift. Against the **drift-matched random baseline**, the flip-up is a statistical
dead-heat: Δ = +3.6 / −5.6 / +2.1 / −61.9 bps at 5/10/20/60 days, and the flip-minus-random
difference **never clears the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar** — the largest |Welch *t*| is **−1.88** at 60
days (*p* = 0.060), and it is **negative** (the flip *underperforms* a dart at 60d). The flip
does not forecast.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — the flip ties or loses to random

| ticker | entries | flip | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (flip−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 238 | +85.2 bps | +2.83 | +106.6 bps | **−21.5 bps** |
| QQQ | 251 | +106.5 bps | +2.88 | +117.0 bps | **−10.5 bps** |
| IWM | 253 | +93.2 bps | +2.44 | +72.5 bps | **+20.6 bps** |
| DIA | 246 | +84.3 bps | +2.56 | +77.7 bps | **+6.7 bps** |
| GLD | 246 | +119.6 bps | +3.34 | +105.8 bps | **+13.8 bps** |

The deltas scatter around zero (−21.5 to +20.6 bps), three positive and two negative, none large
— no coherent, cross-sectional edge. The hefty one-sample *t*'s (every name clears 2) are the
same drift the random baseline already prices in.

## Timing placebo — move the flip to random days, nothing changes

The decisive "does the flip's *timing* matter?" test: keep the **number** of flip-up entries and
the price **marginal**, but draw the entry dates uniformly at random. If the flip genuinely timed
the start of trends, scrambling the dates would collapse the result.

| test | observed flip 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY shuffled-flip timing | +85.2 bps | **0.629** | 500 |

**63% of random-date draws match or beat the real flip** (*p* = 0.629). The flip's timing carries
no information — any set of buy-days does just as well. "The flip forecasts trend" is busted.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real trend

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* post-flip continuation (knob `edge`), the same flip-up
rule behaves exactly as it must — so the flat real-tape result is a genuine "nothing there", not
a dead detector.

| planted edge | n | flip | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no trend) | 151 | −9.5 bps | 48% | −0.22 |
| **0.60** (real planted trend) | 68 | +888.6 bps | 85% | **+9.37** |

With no planted trend the control sits at *t* ≈ 0 (no false positive); a real planted
continuation lights up at *t* = +9.37 with an 85% win-rate. The detector is live.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The flip-up does **not** beat a drift-matched random baseline
  (flip − random = +3.6 / −5.6 / +2.1 / −61.9 bps at 5/10/20/60 days; the flip-vs-random
  Welch *t* never clears 2, and its largest magnitude is **−1.88** at 60 days, *p* = 0.060 —
  *negative*). The impressive one-sample *t*'s (20-day +6.20, 60-day +6.24) are pure beta —
  the upward drift of long equity indices.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no residual edge once the drift you were always getting is
  removed, and costs only deepen the hole. The same drift is captured more cheaply and more
  fully by holding the index; the flip rule trades less and pays costs on each flip, dominating
  nothing. No capacity question because there is no edge to scale.
- **"The flip forecasts trend"? — BUSTED.** The shuffled-flip timing placebo leaves the result
  intact (*p* = 0.629): random buy-days do as well as the real flips, so the activator's flip
  carries no forecasting information. The Gann Hi-Lo Activator is a trailing-stop *drawing* tool,
  not a forecasting strategy.
